sentences: For my ozonated zeolite, I mix the powder into water and use an ozone-water purifier in a glass vessel because ozone destroys plastic.
I mean ozonating water, never inhaling ozone gas.
With a machine producing about two grams of ozone per hour, ten minutes produced a working zeolite for me.
Less time did not work as well, and more time did not noticeably improve it.
I also keep zeolite away from metal during preparation.
Zeolite adsorbs metals, which is part of why it is used for heavy-metal removal, and I don't want it sitting against a metal vessel or utensil before ingestion.
I use glass for ozonation and storage whenever possible.

haiku: Its sentences run at a steady middle length, each beat ending on a tidy summary, and the metals clause reads like a reference passage; the measured trial figures and the first-person test results keep the voice of someone who did the work.
sonnet: Every sentence is complete, orderly and fully explained, with each choice followed by its reason, so the paragraph reads like a procedure written to pre-empt reader questions. The rhythm is even, with medium-length declaratives and no digressions, false starts or loose ends.
